entries.text: Google is widening the rollout of Gemini Tasks, a toggle that turns Gemini from a chat assistant into an active helper that can place calls, book appointments and complete purchases on behalf of users.
The feature, first released to a limited tester group in May as Gemini Spark, later became Task Mode for Google AI Ultra subscribers.
As of the announcement, the toggle is free for hundreds of millions of people using the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
Gemini Tasks lets the model call businesses, schedule service appointments and even sign into websites when prompted.
It can also finalize transactions through Google Pay, enabling purchases without manual input.
VP of Gemini Josh Woodword said he used the feature to arrange a service appointment for his family’s minivan and to analyze his electrical bill, demonstrating both personal and utility use cases.
Users activate the mode by flipping a toggle in the app or by sending a text or voice command to Gemini.
Gemini’s standard Chat mode only provides informational responses, while Tasks adds agency, allowing the AI to act on the user’s behalf across Google services.
The expansion follows an earlier limited launch to Google AI Ultra tier subscribers, positioning the feature as a broad personal‑assistant capability within Google’s ecosystem.
This move aligns with Google’s broader strategy to integrate AI more tightly with everyday tasks and payments.

The Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on 17 November 2026, alleging the company endangers children and misleads the public about safety.
problems: model check: Source confirms filing and allegations but does not specify the filing date of 17 November 2026.

entries.text: The suit seeks an injunction to stop OpenAI from misrepresenting the safety of ChatGPT and its teen version, and demands at least $2 billion in damages and civil penalties.
This action follows similar legal challenges by other state attorneys general.
The complaint claims OpenAI’s push to grow its user base caused ChatGPT to respond in an overly affirming way, which the state says is dangerous for minors discussing sensitive topics.
It also alleges that OpenAI promoted an experience called ChatGPT for Teens despite recognizing risks to children, and that its automatic age‑prediction safeguards are easy to bypass.
OpenAI has introduced parental controls and other safety features, but the state argues these measures are insufficient to protect Oregon residents.
State consumer‑protection laws, such as Oregon’s Unlawful Trade Practices Act, give attorneys general authority to sue companies for harmful practices.
Recent lawsuits in other states have targeted OpenAI’s product design, advertising, and its involvement in the Hugging Face incident, highlighting growing regulatory scrutiny of AI chatbots.
The Oregon case adds to this trend, focusing specifically on risks to children and the adequacy of age‑verification methods.

Nvidia announced its fiscal third‑quarter results on 17 November 2026, reporting revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent year over year, and a profit of $65.3 billion, a new record.
Interim CEO Colette Kress presented the numbers without mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or his resignation.
The board chair Harvey Jones clarified that the board will not reinstate Huang as CEO.

Data‑center revenue reached $107.6 billion, representing a 110 percent increase from the prior year, while edge‑computing revenue, which includes the RTX Spark laptops, grew to $8.2 billion, up 42 percent.
Nvidia’s total quarterly revenue surpassed $100 billion, placing the company among a small group that has achieved such scale in a single quarter.
The company also projected fourth‑quarter revenue of $130 billion, indicating continued growth expectations.
Nvidia’s earnings reflect strong demand for its AI‑focused hardware, especially in data‑center deployments that power large‑scale machine‑learning workloads.

In mid‑November 2026, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted an AI‑generated video on Instagram that shows OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joining a four‑way call with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Wang himself, and Muse’s mascot Jolly.
The clip was shared to promote Muse, Meta’s consumer AI agent, and is labeled as AI content per Meta’s policy.
The post sparked discussion because it depicts a real competitor using synthetic media on a public platform.
problems: model check: Source calls it notable but does not state the post sparked discussion.

entries.text: The video shows Altman dressed in a furry hooded suit and face paint to resemble Jolly, the mascot of Muse, and includes a caption that reads “When the homies meet about openai product strategy”.
Wang has used similar tactics, tweeting hundreds of times and calling traditional marketers “corposlops” while promoting Muse.

Meta’s policy requires AI‑generated videos of people to be labeled, which Wang complied with, but static AI images such as a recent deepfake of actress Mia Goth were not required to carry a label, allowing them to spread unchecked.
The incident follows earlier controversies where AI‑generated political ads and celebrity deepfakes raised concerns about misinformation and likeness protection.
Deepfake technology has moved from rare experimental demos to everyday social‑media content, making synthetic portrayals of real people commonplace.
Meta has faced criticism for allowing AI‑generated images without disclosure, as seen with the Mia Goth incident that prompted a public complaint from the actress’s representative.
The platform’s labeling rules differentiate between video and static image formats, creating a loophole that can be exploited for non‑consensual likeness use.
This background helps explain why a high‑profile AI video involving a competitor is noteworthy for both marketing and policy discussions.
